utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is cross-examining. Now, before we proceed, the Trial Chamber has a ruling on the use of the statements recorded by the Prosecution investigators, such as the one the witness made which the Prosecution is desirous of using in cross-examination. The Trial Chamber has inquired on the record. It shows that Dr. Blagoje Simic surrendered on 12th March, 2001. Prior to that surrender, Mr. Pantelic was lead counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic. So at the time documents including this statement were served, it was during the time that Mr. Pantelic was lead counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic. And on the service of documents, the documents are served on the accused through counsel. When Mr. Pantelic became counsel for Dr. Blagoje Simic, the Prosecution was required to disclose documents regarding Dr. Blagoje Simic at that time. The Trial Chamber is of the view that in order to ensure a fair trial, the statement cannot be used for the reasons that all the evidence adduced using that statement -- all the evidence adduced using that statement will be disregarded. As this is a joint trial, the evidence on record would be considered with respect to all the accused persons. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Omeranovic. I trust that you have rested over the weekend. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence on Friday was that you were a member of the 4th Detachment from I think the end of December 1991 through sometime in 1992. And that you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that my colleague is misquoting what the witness said. He said from January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not important. I'm just taking the witness back to the fact that he was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember the 4th Detachment in the beginning of 1992, Mr. Omeranovic? That was your evidence on Friday. I think you said you were the commander of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The situation with weapons distribution to members of the 4th Detachment was that there was no central warehouse for keeping weapons in Bosanski Samac once so issued, was there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time that we got weapons during a military exercise near Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was: There was no -- once the weapons were issued to the members of the 4th Detachment they kept them at home, didn't they, because there was no place to keep them in Bosanski Samac, that is, no central storage place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said to you that we got weapons near Brcko, we, the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm asking you about is where they were kept. Members of the 4th Detachment kept them at home, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Some of the weapons were issued to platoon or company commanders who distributed them to their troops, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Everyone who had a weapon in the 4th Detachment was issued with a permit, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: These permits were signed by Colonel Nikolic in advance, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it that Colonel Nikolic or someone in his command gave the presigned weapons permits to company and platoon commanders to give to their troops upon issue of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who issued the weapons permits, that's the presigned one that Nikolic had signed? Who issued those to the troops or the members of the 4th Detachment upon receiving their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment they got the weapons, they got these permits, too, these certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment who kept their weapons at home, of course, included company and platoon commanders. That is, you all kept your weapons at home, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I said that last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Some members of the 4th Detachment kept more than one weapon, military-issued weapon, in their home, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have to object because how could the witness possibly answer to this question, "some members." If this could be more specific as whether he knows about such a thing and something like that, whether he kept more than one or someone he knows. But "some members," is just not clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness can answer the question, Your Honour, as to whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re, it's better to be specific what are the names of those people. You first ask him whether he knows whether some members of the 4th Detachment kept more than one weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, are you aware of members of the 4th Detachment keeping more than one military-issued weapon in their home?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had a platoon, and that the only weapons they had were automatic rifles, nothing else. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Over the course of the last few years, you have been interviewed by Defence lawyers and investigators, haven't you? Do you understand my question? Over the last few years, Defence lawyers or investigators have interviewed you, taken statements from you in relation to this case, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the course of your conversations with investigators or Defence lawyers, have you told them that it was a frequent, normal occurrence for the trucks going to the marketplace bringing goods there to park near your house?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not get out of my yard. These people who came to the marketplace left their trucks parked in front of my house and down the entire street. But this was during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just excuse me for one moment. I just want to check the transcript. It may take me a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, on Friday, I asked you, this is at page 82, line 7 of the transcript, for everyone's benefit, I said: "And trucks frequently park in the vicinity of your house delivering their produce to markets, don't they"? Your answer was: "Sir, the markets is 50 metres from me. In my street, it was forbidden to park vehicles regardless of whether they were passenger or freight vehicles. You were allowed to -- not park, and parking was defined as stopping for more than 15 minutes." Do you remember that question and answer on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Friday --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's why the police intervened, and they had to leave those spaces that were not parking spaces to begin with, but in order to unload their goods, people would stop there for about 10 minutes or whatever, unload their goods, and then they would proceed. They were not supposed to park there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify. On Friday, your answer suggested that trucks didn't park there because they weren't allowed to. Today, a moment ago, you just told us that people were -- you could not get out of your yard. "These people that came to the marketplace left their trucks in front of my house and down the entire street." What I want to ask you is why, when I asked you on Friday trucks -- just wait a minute, please. When I suggested to you the trucks parked in front of your house, you didn't just simply say yes, they did, preventing me from getting out of my yard. Instead, you told the Trial Chamber that trucks were not allowed to park there. Why the difference in the two accounts, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's different, sir. I mean, this is what the rules are in our part of the world in traffic. At places where one is not allowed to park, one may stop, though, but after 15 minutes, it's considered to be parking. I did not say that stopping was forbidden, but parking is forbidden, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just take you back to the question I asked a moment ago which was: Did you tell the lawyers or investigators for the Defence that it was a frequent, normal occurrence for those trucks to bring goods to that marketplace and stay parked there? That's all I want to know. Is that what you told them during the course of your conversations with the Defence lawyers or investigators?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody even asked me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Friday, this is at page 73 of the transcript, about line 5, Mr. Lazarevic asked you: "At any point in time did you together with Mr. Simo Zaric in that street in front of your house -- or rather in front of your mother's house, did you unload boxes of military weapons from a truck and carry it into your backyard?" Your answer to the question was: "Let me tell you, sir, I've already said what the ethnic composition was in my street. Had I taken a bottle of whiskey and carried it through the street, and carried it into -- it into my home, everybody would have seen it, even if I carried it in a shopping bag. But two trucks, two trucks, that is so absurd. First of all, I would not allow any such thing to happen in front of my house, and it didn't happen." Now, that was the question Mr. Lazarevic asked you, and that was the answer you gave. Mr. Lazarevic asked you about a truck, but you responded by saying two trucks and repeating it. Why, sir, when he asked you about a truck did you respond by saying two trucks, two trucks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, but I have to say one thing to my colleague. While preparing and proofing with this witness, I quoted him --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. I've put a question to the witness. My learned friend is cluing him. I'm asking him about his answer on Friday. That's not a proper objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I'll allow Mr. Lazarevic to complete his objection if he still wants to put it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he's going to put words in the witness's mouth or provide an explanation which the witness can give, I would object to him giving that explanation. If he's objecting on the basis of relevance or form or some of the legitimate basis for objecting, of course I don't object to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'll allow counsel to put up his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while proofing with this witness, there was some parts of transcript where his name was mentioned by witness Nusret Hadzijusufovic, and while preparing this witness, I quoted him, I read him these relevant parts of transcript where it was said that there were two trucks, and this is what I discussed with this witness while preparing this. Maybe this can give an explanation to my learned colleague how come it was mentioned. Maybe my question, the way I understand what my colleague said, it was probably my question that was problematic for the witness. I said "trucks." Maybe I did say "truck" or "trucks," but it was really nothing that should mislead this witness because he was familiar with the transcript excerpts where his name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re and to the witness also, the witness under solemn declaration to tell the truth, so there should be no problem. You can continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is this: On Friday, Mr. Lazarevic asked you about a truck. Your response was, you spoke about a shopping bag, but two trucks, and you repeated it. "Two trucks, that is so absurd." What I want to know is: Why, when Mr. Lazarevic asked you about one truck, a truck, you responded by saying two trucks and repeating it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely for the reason that the Defence counsel explained to you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is that that Mr. Lazarevic told you in proofing you or in conference that there were -- the allegation was two trucks? And when he asked you about one truck, you decided to answer it by saying two trucks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say this to you: I don't even remember that I said "two," but let it be. Maybe I did. Two trucks, I mean, the way that witness put it...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest that what happened was that in early April 1992, during the night, two trucks arrived outside your house. There were two men there, and you and Mr. Zaric were present when they unloaded a box from the car -- sorry, from the truck, and the two men carried it into your backyard or your mother's backyard carrying a box which had rope handles on it. I suggest that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence on Friday was that you had worked for the Red Cross from just after when you had been released from detention, along the lines of you had run into a friend --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was that you had run into a friend who offered me a sort of job at the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to show you a document, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in respect of this document, I have just received it 20 minutes ago, just before these proceedings started this morning. I didn't have time to discuss this document with the witness. I have no problem with the contents of this documents. Furthermore, it is -- in fact, it is proving what the witness said according to the date when he did start working for the Red Cross. But I just want it for the record that this document was never discussed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution responds by saying it's a Red Cross document, and the Prosecution had no reason to, (a), look for the document or, (b), disclose it until the witness gave evidence on Friday that he had worked for the Red Cross because it wasn't in the summary which was provided and filed with the Court. There was no mention of the Red Cross. And we didn't find out until Friday that there was going to be evidence on the Red Cross, and as a result of this, the document appeared. It's an identical document to D1413, I think. And except it has this man's name on it instead of someone else's. In fact, the case manager, Mr. Leese, has just reminded me that it was in fact disclosed by the Defence last year because it bears a Y number. The simple reason why we hadn't disclosed it before because we had no reason to. I understand there's no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic simply stated that he wanted to put it on record that he just received this document. Now, Mr. Re, what is the position? Is the position that because it bears a Y number, that means it was disclosed last year? Is that the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. If it has a Y number, then it was disclosed by the Defence. That's what Mr. Leese tells me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It is a document which comes from the Defence to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, last year. That's my instructions on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may give just one brief answer. First of all, the Prosecution here referred on a number of occasions during its cross-examination to the statement that this witness gave to the investigators of the Prosecution. And looking through this statement, it is quite obvious, on page 2, that the witness said: "A friend of mine came and asked me to work for the Red Cross." So this was not the first time that the Prosecution heard from this witness that he worked for the Red Cross. They already had this information back in 1998, if I am correct when this statement was given. One second, in 1998. And the other thing is that this document I've seen here for the first time. As I already said, I have no problem with the content of this document and the dates and everything. This is truly the very same document as we had for Witness Svetozar Vasovic, the form is the same, everything is the same, except for the name of this witness and the date is different when he started working for the Red Cross. But I just want to say this particular document, we haven't received as the Defence of Mr. Zaric, and this is the first time that we have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, what the Prosecution is saying is that because of the labelling of it, that is a document which came from the Defence, which was disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I can assure the Trial Chamber is that we didn't have this document. The Defence of Mr. Zaric, we did not disclose this document to the Prosecution. This is what I can say on behalf of Mr. Zaric's document. Otherwise, we would tender it into evidence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was apparently one of 464 documents which Mr. Di Fazio received from the Defence, I can't tell you exactly who from, in July -- I think the 25th of July, 1991. 1991, yes. 1991. I'm sorry, I've given you the wrong date. 25th of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The records I have with me don't reveal it, but -- Mr. Lazarevic doesn't object to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I think these are documents by the Red Cross that the Defence for Mr. Tadic disclosed to the Prosecution. It is a set of several Red Cross documents that we have disclosed, but we haven't been using them. We haven't tendered them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, you see that document there. It's a document issued by the Serbian municipality of Samac Red Cross Crisis Staff. And you can see from the document it's a work obligation assignment for you dated the 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, I have seen this document for the first time in July when the general mobilisation was being carried out, and there, at the time, it was said that whoever held this type of a document did not have to respond to the mobilisation callup. I went to the Red Cross then and asked if I had such a document. And the man working there gave me this particular document, and that was the first time I had seen it. And I used it at the time for that particular reason, not to have to respond to the mobilisation callup. And as for this date, well it could be the 20th or the 30th written here on this particular document, but what is true is that I started working -- working as soon as I came out of the prison, and not just me, there were many of us, Muslims, Bosniaks, and we were working in the streets, in the crossroads, where we were distributing bread and milk to the citizens. It wasn't just me. There was over 20 of us. It was only later that I got this. I didn't even know that I was admitted into the Red Cross under the work obligation. It was only after I had seen this document that I realised this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May the document be tendered into evidence. We only have a B/C/S at the moment. We will have it translated straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification until we receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be treated P173 ter IT.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You can see from the document, Mr. Omeranovic, it refers to you having -- receiving a work obligation on the 19th of April. That date is consistent with when you started, just the date, isn't it? Within a few days, the date on the document, 19th of April, is consistent with when you started working with the Red Cross, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working before then reflected on this document. Well, anyway, I was lucky to have received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is: You were in custody on the 17th or the 18th. This document is dated the 19th. Your evidence was that you started working with the Red Cross almost as soon as you got out of -- as soon as you were released from custody. The date there is consistent with about the time when you started working for the Red Cross to within a couple of days, isn't it? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what you're saying, this is true, but not according to what I know. I was supposed to obviously start working on this date, and it seems to me that it was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know who arranged for your work obligation through the Red Cross, given that that document says it was a work obligation? Do you know who's responsible for arranging it? If you don't, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one really arranged it. It wasn't just me there. There were other Bosniaks. Whoever they needed was taken on. But I think that whoever worked also had this type of a document. I cannot speak for the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your work at the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you should be winding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You started on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm only asking about the Red Cross because it was raised in examination-in-chief, and that wasn't taken account of when Your Honours set the cross-examination time limits. And there is a link between the Red Cross and other aspects of the indictment which I just briefly wish to ask the witness about if he knows, and only because it was raised in examination-in-chief, not in the summary we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You better move fast, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your work at the Red Cross, Mr. Omeranovic, did you -- did it involve visiting prisoners in detention centres? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your work at the Red Cross have anything to do with exchanges or lists of people for exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever to do with that. I wasn't doing that type of work. As I told you, for a while, we were distributing bread and milk. Afterwards, I left the Red Cross, and then when I came back again I performed all sorts of manual-types of jobs, unloading trucks, whatever was actually the hardest work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of how the Red Cross operated in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you said that you left the Red Cross. Where did you go when you left the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the factory where I worked before. Because I was -- I received a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you went to the factory, was that a work obligation assignment you received, to go and work in the factory?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you about -- finally, I want to take you back very briefly to the arrest. As far as you know, your name wasn't on any list of people to be arrested or of people who may have had illegal weapons, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, in April 1992, your name wasn't on a list of people who had weapons, which they had illegally acquired in the hands of the people who were doing the arrests, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: No one ever told you your name was on a list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever told me anything. I was just arrested, beaten up, taken away, and detained. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you finished the Red Cross extension which you said wasn't in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is my question last, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, Mr. Omeranovic, your arrest was a mistake and was probably only because you're a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was a member of the 4th Detachment because they were arresting some Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask him how many Serbs he knows of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re. You keep on extending your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's just the one issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, he raised something in the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you please sit down, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to sit down. I just want to put on the record I just wanted to ask him who these Serbs were. That was the only thing I wanted to ask him, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that the Prosecution has introduced a document disclosed to them by the Defence for Mr. Tadic, I would like to put some questions to the witness relating to these documents and relating to the questions put to the witness by the Prosecution relating to this document. I would kindly ask the witness to be shown the Document P --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the number. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Omeranovic, good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P173 ID. That was the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, my name is Dragan Krgovic, and I will put to you several questions on behalf of the Defence for Mr. Tadic relating to the document you have just seen. When you were answering the questions by the Prosecutor, if I understood you well, can you tell me precisely when was it that you started working for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I left the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw this document only in the month of July?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, would you be so kind as to read this document carefully. Does the document mention the term "work obligation," or does it only say "assignment to different jobs and tasks"? This because the Prosecutor used the term "work obligation" when putting his question to you. And I haven't really read the contents of the document. Could you please read this first paragraph under this decision. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Assignment of workers to jobs of the Serbian Red Cross in the staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac." Is this what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Does this document mention anywhere the term "work obligation"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I don't need this document. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Omeranovic, the Prosecutor asked you about the statement you gave to the OTP investigators on the 27th of November of 1998, and the Prosecutor quoted certain parts of the statement asking you whether you said something like that to the investigators. Now I would kindly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has just made the ruling this morning that the evidence adduced by using that statement to be disregarded because of the fact that it wasn't served on Mr. Blagoje Simic and the fact that as this is a joint trial, any evidence will be taken into consideration for all the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. What I wanted to quote to the witness had nothing to do with Mr. Blagoje Simic. This was something related strictly to Mr. Simo Zaric, but if this is the ruling, then I won't have any questions, any redirect for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. While we are waiting for the next witness, may I briefly address the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it to do with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Wait, I'll give you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I brief the Chamber concerning the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't want the next witness delayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you want to say is concerning the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pasaga Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been given 20 minutes cross-examination for Pasaga Tihic, and the Prosecution had a proposal. The next witness, as I said, has been given 20 minutes cross after 40 minutes of examination-in-chief. My next witness after Pasaga Tihic is Peta Kalavic. This witness is a 92 bis witness who I will either cross-examine for one hour tomorrow or Wednesday morning based on how the schedule proceeds. This -- Your Honour, if I have to make an offer of proof I'd like to make it outside the presence of the witness, unless he not put his headphones on and he doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe he can just wait outside the courtroom just by the door, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As I said, the next witness that I have to cross-examine after this witness will be tomorrow, which is we have been given one hour, which is Peta Kalavic, a 92 bis witness. The witness today has given two statements, one to the OTP, a six-page, single-spaced statement and a two-page statement to some investigators in Orasje, not OTP investigation. He was originally a witness for the Prosecution. What the Prosecution would like to do is take the one hour from Peta Kalavic and use that to cross-examine this witness, and Peta Kalavic which is a 92 bis witness which we barely feel we have no cross-examination for just use the 20 minutes tomorrow or the following day for that witness. This specific witness here can assist in many topics. He is the sole witness concerning certain incidents or one of two or three witnesses that witnessed certain evidence. He provides evidence -- rebuttal-type evidence to people such as Naser Sejdic, who was the police officer, who was the Muslim police officer who worked at the SUP under Stevan Todorovic and testified two days ago. But utilising this witness Pasaga Tihic, it doesn't require us to call a witness in rebuttal. We can use him as one of the few witnesses who stayed a long time at the high school. We've had a lot of testimony from people who stayed at the SUP, the Territorial Defence building, and the primary school. This is one of the few witnesses we've had throughout the trial who has stayed at the high school. He is one of the few if any of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. He's one of the few of any witnesses to the statements that Simo Zaric made concerning Namik Suljic. He's a witness in relation to actions that he has seen Blagoje Simic commit. He is a witness as to actions of Simo Zaric. He is a witness as to actions at the radio station. He is a witness as to information relating to the famous Novi Sad television programme, what happened to the tape of that programme, and how the tape, the audiotape was then used in Bosanski Samac. As a result, we're not asking for additional time and to extend the trial. We just want to take the witness that I'll have to cross-examine tomorrow or Wednesday morning, Peta Kalavic who has been given one hour, it's a 92 bis witness statement with a one-hour cross-examination. I only need 10 to 20 minutes on that. Give the 20 minutes for this witness, Peta Kalavic, and let me take the one hour for Peta Kalavic and use it today. I've notified Defence counsel who was producing this witness of this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Before you sit down, I just want to know about the statements the witness made. Do they fall in the same category?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. The major statement, the OTP statement has been provided to all counsel. I have the receipts signed by counsel. The second statement I provided yesterday. I am not introducing the second statement. There's a couple phrases I might question him on basically just to refresh his recollection. I don't have really any use for the second statement. The first statement is extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber agrees to give you the time that you have asked for in exchange for the time for the witness you mentioned Peta Kalavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one clarification. The Prosecutor is speaking of two statements given by this witness. We received from the Prosecution in the reciprocal disclosure a statement by this witness while he was on the list of Prosecution witnesses. And now the second statement mentioned by the Prosecutor is something we have never received. We have received the statement yesterday, and an official proffer written by a person after the interview with Mr. Pasaga Tihic. And I would kindly ask my learned colleague to tell me which is the other witness? Is it -- this other statement done not by the OTP but by someone else or is there a third actually statement, some third document that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm referring to the statement that was taken in Orasje by Zvonko Susic, which I provided yesterday. I'm not introducing the statement. I'm not going to use it to impeach him. The most I would do is refresh his recollection if there's any question that he cannot recall a certain fact. But most of my -- just about all of my cross-examination will concern the first statement, just information that he has previously provided, which he has sworn to, which he has signed, and he has initialled every single page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I have this statement here. It is not a statement by Pasaga Tihic. There are no initials of his. These are just some official notes done by a third person from Derventa. His name is Zvonko Susic who made some sort of a notation which has not been signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Counsel might be confused. That's the new statement, the two-page statement, which I'm barely going to use. I might just refresh a witness's recollection with it. The key statement is the statement that was given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What Mr. Krgovic is saying is that statement, the second one, is not a statement by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They are notes by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's an investigator's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then it's not a statement of the witness, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what my intervention was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because if it's the investigator's notes, then it can't be used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, the only thing it could be used is to refresh his recollection, do you recall discussing this? Does this refresh your recollection that you discussed this, witness, and you said the following? Does that refresh your recollection? Can you now recall after hearing that? Whatever question I asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there any record that the notes were read back to him, the normal things? Because what we are against is holding a witness to notes by somebody else because the notes are made by somebody else according to their own understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no, all I would use that for, Your Honour, if I said to him: Do you know John Smith -- and I'll just use an example, Do you know John Smith, and he says, I don't recall. I could show him his statement and refresh his recollection, remember, you made a previous statement about John Smith and you said X, does that now refresh your recollection that you know John Smith and anything about him? He can either say yes or he can say no. If he says no, I go on to another subject. It's just to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think there's just one sort of problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: His interview. I use the word "statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You used the word "statement" again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I could show him his previous interview. In fact, under the doctrine of refreshing recollection you can use anything, including the old joke which is in the English case books you can use a banana. If you show someone a banana and they say yes now they recall whatever previous facts they previously said, that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Weiner. You can bring the witness in. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness makes the solemn declaration and before he enters, I'd just like to say that we have been caught rather by surprise with this request of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... And don't give him the earphones, first. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are taken quite by surprise in this situation when proofing this witness and deciding to call this witness under Rule 71, in this, we base ourselves on the fact that the OTP has not called this man as his witness, and we told the witness on his way here that the Chamber had decided to hear his testimony only with reference to a particular part of events, and that is how the witness was proofed. And it was said then that the OTP would examine Mr. Tihic during a time that you had set aside for it, that is, 20 minutes, half of the time that had been allotted to us for the examination-in-chief. I mean, I only wish the Trial Chamber to bear this in mind, but in principle, your decision is there. And I shall naturally be guided by your instructions and directions at the time when we were taking these statements under Rule 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, the Trial Chamber doesn't find anything prejudicial to your case by allowing the Prosecution to have more time to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I fully agree with you, and I do not think it will be prejudicial to Mr. Zaric's Defence, and we merely wished to draw your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after the witness makes the solemn declaration, I will start my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we shall go ahead. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tihic. I'm sorry about this to and froing that happened. I will only inform you before we begin properly that the Trial Chamber [as interpreted] has been allowed to examine you for one hour. This is merely by way of information. And we shall now move within the boundaries of the examination for which you were called by Mr. Zaric's Defence. As we were getting ready for this, I gave you some instructions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just a little intervention, in your question, "the Trial Chamber," you say, "has been allowed to examine the witness for one hour." I think you mean the Prosecutor, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that the Trial Chamber has decided that the Prosecutor should be granted one hour for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That clarifies it because there were obviously words missed out in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, well it must have been some misunderstanding with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So wait for my question to finish. If something is not clear, then tell me once again to rephrase my question, and I'll do that. But it is very important for you to speak slowly and clearly, because it is important to record your testimony in the transcript so that it remains just the way that you testified here.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, please, will you tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Pasaga Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1961.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us where were you born?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Slavonski Brod," your birthplace, where is it, in which former republic of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian Republic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 10, question and answer have not been divided. After the question, will you tell us where you were born? Slavonski Brod was the answer of the witness. It is not quite clear here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the problem was that there was no pause between the questions and the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just wait a little after you've heard my question, and then answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said you were born in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In which of the republics of former Yugoslavia is Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us something about your education.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I've come from the electrical engineering school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete that school?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you married, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where do you live now, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In Slovenia, in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where do your parents live?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In Samac, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what do you do now for a living?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I have a company in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what is it into?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: By and large, equipment of petrol stations, publicity ads, but mostly things that have to do with petrol stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever serve the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to tell us which political party were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: The SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did you live in Bosanski Samac prior to the conflict in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Let me see, 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, earlier on, when you lived in Bosanski Samac prior to -- until 1992, did you ever work and were you employed by the Bosanski Samac radio station?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, will you tell us what was your job there and what is it that you did at the Bosanski Samac radio station prior to 1992? How many years were you employed with it and what kind of jobs did you hold there?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: The job was an engineering job, a technician working with mixing equipment. And at the same time, I was also involved in the production of programmes, and I was also a disk jockey. I chose the music. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us how long did you do this?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I did it for about nine years. Practically from the time when the radio station was opened in the Memorial Centre until I got a new job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That radio station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think it's important in view of what the witness will be discussing, up to when did he leave the job? Because it simply says: "Until I got a new job." We would like to know when he stopped working at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means. By all means, Your Honour. And this was going to be precisely the next question that I was -- that I wanted to ask. But I merely wanted to establish the fact and ask Mr. Tihic, because he knows it, which were the wavelengths of the Bosanski Samac radio station prior to 1992. And my next question was to be: When did you cease working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So will you please be so kind as to tell us what were the wavelengths of the Bosanski Samac radio stations?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: We had UHF, it had two transmitters, a medium waves and the UKT transmitter. The latter was in the building itself, and the medium wave was a couple of hundred metres away, that is, located in the primary school in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that, where did you go then? What was your next workplace and when did you change the company?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I went to a different company about a year before the conflict, which means sometime around 1990, early 1991. And I went to join Elektrodistribucija, the power distribution company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The events in Samac on the 16th and 17th, at that time you were where? At the Elektrodistribucija Bosanski Samac, isn't it, that is where you worked at the time?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when were you arrested and who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 18th of April, 1992, and I was arrested by those in many coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After that arrest, did you work at the Bosanski Samac radio station? Tell us, please, if you did, then how did that come about? How did it come about that you found yourself once again performing a job at the radio station?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: After I was arrested on the 18th of April, I was taken to the TO offices, the Territorial Defence, the home guard offices. And the next day, so it should be around the 20th of April, they came to take me to the police offices, SUP or MUP, where I was detained. And there were two men in many coloured uniforms there waiting for me. They only had nicknames, Beli and Debeli. And they started beating me there, asking for a Mercedes which I used to drive before the war broke out. And as -- when I told them where the Mercedes was and what had happened to it, and so they left that room and went to the adjoining one, and presumably somebody there confirmed my statements, and then they let me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who did you meet then and whom did you go to visit?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Then, when they let me go, Stevan Todorovic asked me to come to his office. That was the adjoining room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Stevan Todorovic tell you then?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: He told me to go to the radio station without delay, since something was wrong with the programme there. Or, as he put it, something was wrong with the radio station's work and that I should go there, report to the editor, the then editor, and my former editor, Mr. Vaso Antic. And if I failed to do that, or if I escaped, they knew that my parents were at home, my father, mother, and all the other members of my family, my sister, too, and that they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you also obligated to report to the police station daily?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: After I went and reported to Vaso Antic, the then editor, I was also obligated to report to the police station three times a day, and there was always the threat if I escape, my parents are at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you came, and did you report to the editor Vaso Antic, and what did you establish as you -- when you went to the radio station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went there straight away to see Mr. Antic. I reported to him. However, since I saw with my own eyes, as I had spent nine years working at that place, I saw that at the mixing device, I could see that the medium wave transmitter was not operational, or rather that the frequency which covered the wide area of Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And which was the frequency of the Radio Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: It used UKT transmitter. It was the ultrashort waves, and it covered only the central part of the town. But basically, the ultrashort waves still covered part of the town and also switched on the transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you establish?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I went to the site, and since I said that the medium-wave transmitter was not far from the radio station's building, and I could see that a part of the school building which housed the medium-wave transmitter had not been damaged or rather had not been set on fire because the rest of the school was on fire. And presumably, the firefighters, as they were putting out the fire in the school, had also damaged the medium-wave transmitter by pouring water over it. And when I got there, I saw that the whole transmitter was immersed in water, so naturally it could not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you repair it then?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, by working at night, I put it in order again and I think that two days later, it became operational again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did the coverage of the -- the area covered by Radio Samac increase when this was put back in operation?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that the area covered by it increased by some three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that, what did you do in the radio station itself? What was your job? Will you please describe your tasks.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Every time after I'd report to the SUP building in the morning, I'd go to work in the radio station, and I would air the programme. My task was to see that the radio station works, that it is operational, to broadcast programmes, that is, to broadcast programmes as ordered by the then editor, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could anything be broadcast by Radio Samac without you sitting at the mixing console and do you realize that nothing could have been broadcast without your knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, nothing could be broadcast without my knowing about it. That is, without me switching it on and releasing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And you, of course, controlled the work as the programmes went on, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just add, I was involved in the editing, in the broadcasting, in the removal of -- well, by and large, what the editor told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, what was aired most frequently?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from music, there were various proclamations, information, and such like. But in between and before and after and in between, there was music.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, how long did you go on working for the Bosanski Samac radio station?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: You mean after I was brought there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, following the 17th of April and the 18th of April. When after you were brought there again?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I mean, how many days? Well, about a month. 30 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And as you were there in the radio station in Samac, did you ever see Mr. Simo Zaric be present or visit the offices of Radio Samac or take part in Radio Samac's programmes?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, what do you know about whether you were tasked by your editor to copy some of Mr. Zaric's statements from a video to an audiotape?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not only Mr. Zaric's, but also all the other material that was brought there, that is, I copied it all, and then I broadcast programmes as ordered by Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is now time for our regular break. Mr. Tihic, we shall resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before this break, Mr. Tihic, you spoke about everything you did while you were at the radio -- while you worked at Radio Samac, and you talked about sound mixing and things like that. Now, tell me, do you remember whether you had a videocassette with some interviews that you then taped on to audiotapes? Can you tell us about this, who asked you to do this and what was done generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: One day, Mr. Antic, the editor, brought a videocassette. And he said that the material from that tape should be taken off, and of course, I did that. From the video, I retaped it on to those big professional tapes, Revox, so then we had this entire material retaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Simo Zaric's interview on that tape, the one that he gave to TV Novi Sad? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you then also retape the interviews of other interviewees from that programme, from TV Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: All of it, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was an interview of Mr. Tihic; Omer Nalic; Hadzialijagic, nicknamed Coner; Izetbegovic, do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also said that there was Mr. Omer Nalic's interview, right?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And tell me now, since you were the man in charge of producing this programme, did you play this cassette, the cassette with Mr. Zaric's interview? Was it actually broadcast in the programme?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many times this happened during that one month while you worked at Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after this one month, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, at the very outset when I started working at the radio station, Mr. Todorovic ordered that a man be brought in, a young man who I was supposed to train for working at the radio station. Of course, he was a Serb in terms of his ethnic background. So I did that. To give this information accurately, his first name is Goran, and I think his last name is Bosic. And one day, two policemen came to -- they came after my working hours were over. They came to pick me up. They took me to the high school. I was there among the other prisoners. I was the only Muslim among the Croats who were there. All the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were detained, were you in a position to follow the radio programme of Radio Bosanski Samac and do you know what was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, this was not an opportunity that was given to us, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel? The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tihic. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to be asking you some questions over the next hour. All right? Thank you. Now, let's go back to April 18th when you were arrested by Serb paramilitaries. You were taken to the police station with Ibrahim Salkic. Isn't that correct? Ibela?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you arrive at the police station, you meet with Stevan Todorovic and a paramilitary called Crne?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they give you some orders at that time. They tell you that you and Salkic are to go to the Red Cross building and remove the flag, the Red Cross flag, at the local Red Cross. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they tell the members of the 4th Detachment that are present that they are to escort you on this assignment. Isn't that correct? And when I say "they," Crne and Todorovic tell certain members of the 4th Detachment that they are to escort you on this mission or assignment?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were told, you and Ibela Salkic are told that you are to walk in front of the 4th Detachment members who will be searching for weapons?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you and Salkic, Mr. Salkic follow these instructions from Todorovic and Crne and you leave the police station with 4th Detachment members?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And before leaving the police station, Todorovic gives you some sort of white armband for you and Salkic to wear when you're walking in front of the 4th Detachment members? Correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you walk along the roadway apparently towards the Red Cross building, and there's a group of 4th Detachment members in a Praga that are behind you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you please describe to the Court what this Praga looks like? Was it big? Was it small? Did it have a gun on it? Is it armour plated? Could you please describe to the Court what a Praga looks like.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very knowledgeable as far as these weapons are concerned, but this is an armoured vehicle, and it had a barrel in front. That's about it. Well, it's not like a gun on a tank; it's smaller. It's sort of like on a machine-gun or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. How many 4th Detachment members were escorting you either on the Praga or on foot?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them were in the vehicle, but around the vehicle, I can't remember now exactly how many of them were there. But I don't know. About ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a group of them basically. Now, in addition to the 4th Detachment members that were sent by Todorovic and Crne, were there any paramilitaries, you know, the Serbian paramilitaries, that were also present either on the Praga or in that group that was escorting you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And while you walked to the Red Cross building -- did you eventually get to the Red Cross building and remove the flag, the Red Cross flag?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you carried out this order, you indicated that you stopped at houses where the 4th Detachment members would search for weapons?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just a final few questions on this: You indicated that the Serbian paramilitaries, Laki and Crne's group, were wearing camouflage uniforms and painted faces?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the 4th Detachment members also had some camouflage uniforms and some were in civilian clothing or regular clothes?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated that you were originally in the SUP, and then you get moved to the TO. And around the 20th, the 21st of April, you get called back across the street to the police station. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were originally brought to a group of paramilitaries where you were beaten, and they tried to extort your car or money or whatever from you. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then after you were beaten, you were brought next door to Todorovic's office, to the next office over. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated in your statement that when you were brought there, present in that office were Todorovic, the defendant Simo Zaric, Vlado Sarkanovic, and Milos Culapovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague can clarify that because that is not what we heard here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You previously indicated -- not in your testimony today but in your statement which you had given to the OTP, that when you got to the office, Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric, Milos Culapovic, and Vlado Sarkanovic were all in Stevan Todorovic's office. Is that what you recall?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us who was in the office?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: When those two beat me up, this Beli and Debeli and when they asked for the Mercedes, and when they checked my story, then they ordered this policeman to take me. He took me to Mr. Todorovic's office which was upstairs. When you go upstairs, then it's on the right-hand side. Mr. Todorovic was there, and then he said to me that I should go to report to Mr. Antic at the radio station. And then came all the rest that I already talked about today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But at some time in that office with Stevan Todorovic, you indicate in your statement which you gave to the OTP, Simo Zaric was there, Vlado Sarkanovic was there, and Milos Culapovic was there. Do you recall that? And then you talked to Simo Zaric, and he brings you into another office. Do you recall that? Do you recall those people being present?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Not in the room. Not in the room. Mr. Zaric was not in the room, and Culapovic and Sarkanovic. But as I was walking downstairs, as I was leaving Mr. Todorovic's offices, Mr. Zaric called me into a room that was on the opposite side, on the left side, to show me some documents that he had found. I don't know who found this actually, in this safe box.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The only reason I want to clarify is because in your statement on page 3, you state that: "The next morning I was taken to the SUP where Stiv's office was. There I saw Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric, Vlado Sarkanovic, and Milos Culapovic. Then Simo Zaric took me to a room." So your statement is now that they weren't all together in room. You met them separately at the police station. Isn't that correct? Is that what your testimony is? You saw Stevan Todorovic in the office, and you saw Simo Zaric in the hallway or the stairway?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Simo Zaric brings you to Namik Suljic's office. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Since we knew each other from before, we went hunting together and I don't know what all, I mean together with this Namik Suljic, that's what I wanted to say, he took me to this room next door to show me these documents on which -- in which my name was too allegedly. And then he said to me: Look, Pasaga, we have found these lists of certain individuals from Samac. They were compiled by Alija Fitozovic. I said to him then as well that I have nothing to do with these lists. Actually, nobody asked me whether I wanted to be on these lists or not. That's it. That's the first time that I saw that my name was on some kind of list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he showed you these lists, and was anyone else in the room or was it just you and Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Only the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Simo tells you after he shows you these lists of Muslim and Croat names, and those were the Muslim and Croat names of the persons who were going to establish a military unit or the formation of a military unit. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Simo tells you at that point that if he had found Namik Suljic, he would beat him badly. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group is Namik Suljic a member of?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then after you have this meeting with Simo Zaric, what happens to you next? Do you go back to Stevan Todorovic's office or do you leave for the radio station?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: The radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you go to the radio station to repair equipment, to make sure it's fully functional or operational. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the person in charge of the station is Vaso Antic, and Ljubomir Cordasevic is the reporter.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you're at the station over a period of a month, Stevan Todorovic is calling on a daily basis, sometimes as much as 20 times a day, asking or demanding that Chetnik or Serbian nationalistic songs are to be played. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had no such tapes in the radio station, but Vaso Antic goes out and brings them to the station to play, to play over the air.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, how often were these Chetnik or nationalistic songs played or broadcasted over the air? How often each day?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: All the time, throughout the programme, so between reports, pieces of information that were broadcast before and after that. They were played all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you also listened to some of the broadcasts such as the daily news, different news reports, and proclamations? You were listening to these. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you were listening, especially to the news broadcasts, you were aware that the radio station was supplying false information or propaganda to the public?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was this happening frequently, this false information being supplied to the public? False stories?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you say on a daily basis it was happening?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you ever asked to assist in developing any of these false tapes by adding sound effects or special effects or taping portions of other stories together so they could play some of these false stories?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was producing these false stories or propaganda?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was producing them, but Mr. Antic and Mr. Cordasevic, they were journalists, so they typed these texts out, and then they were read out by a lady announcer.
