utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these false stories or propaganda, these would be used to attempt to legitimise or to minimise certain improper conduct being committed. Would you agree with that? You're nodding your head yes.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were any improper phrases or terms used during these radio broadcasts such as the word "Ustasha"? Was that ever used, "Ustasha" or "Ustasha forces"?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was the phrase "Muslim forces" ever used referring to Muslim armed force -- Muslim soldiers, if you recall? Referring to the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was there ever any discussion of genocide against the Serbian people, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Against the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall those phrases, "genocide against the Serbs," similar to the TV Novi Sad programme where they discussed genocide against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall any mention of the Muslims want to impose Islam on the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, do you recall anything about always mentioning that the Serb forces were defending, and you very rarely ever heard any mention of the Serb forces attacking, they were always defending. Is that consistent with what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: It has been 11 years, you know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. What sort of things do you recall, what sort of false information or propaganda do you recall that was broadcasted over the Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, concerning the number of persons killed, the advancement of the Serb forces, the voluntary surrender. I don't know. Moving out, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- now, the person who replaced you at the radio station, I think you mentioned his name, Goran something, was it?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Goran Bosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group did he belong?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... I don't know why we need to go to this again. The witness has already said in his testimony that he was replaced by a young Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. As long as it's on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, didn't they broadcast at one point that the paramilitaries or the camouflage soldiers, Crne and company, Crne, Luga, Laki, Zvezdan, were not people from Serbia, but were really people who had been born right in the Bosanski Samac municipality? Didn't they even broadcast something to that extent?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that wasn't true, having lived there for 30 years?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did the radio station or the reporter from the radio station, didn't he cover civilian authority meetings such as Executive Board meetings, Crisis Staff meetings, and when I say "covered," didn't he attend and take notes to make reports?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the meetings that this -- do you know -- I'm sorry, let me start again. Do you know where the meetings were held that he was covering or that he would -- that the reporter would attend and take notes?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: He would go to the Crisis Staff, that is, rather, when I was on my way to report to SUP in the morning, Mr. Antic and Cordasevic went to the municipality to obtain some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you had to report to the SUP, the SUP or the police station, three times a day. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And directly next to the SUP is the municipal building. If you're facing the SUP, it's just to the left?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would accompany Mr. Antic and -- what's Ljubomir's -- how do you pronounce his last name?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Cordasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would accompany Mr. Antic sometimes and Mr. Cordasevic to that area, the police station, municipal building. Isn't that correct? Or you would all arrive at the same time? You would see each other there?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: When I would be leaving my house, because I spent nights at home, and then I would report to the SUP in the morning. And going from my house, I would have to actually pass by the municipality building to get to the SUP in order to report. And I did meet on several occasions when they were on their way to the municipal building and I was on my way to SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that time, when you were going to the SUP and passing the municipal building, you were aware that there was a Serbian Crisis Staff that had taken control of the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that Blagoje Simic was the president of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you were in that vicinity of the police station or municipal building - let's just take the vicinity of the municipal building - did you ever see Blagoje Simic or any other Crisis Staff or Executive Board members enter, any civilian officials, entering that municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, maybe first our colleague should establish whether the witness knows who were the other members, before he answers this question. He said that he was aware that Mr. Blagoje Simic was the president of the Crisis Staff. But when he asks him other members...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness is capable of answering whether he knew them or not. He will give that answer to the Prosecution. There's no need for interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, first, did you see any civilian officials entering the municipal building during that time?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Both civilians and uniformed people entered the building. I don't know who you mean. Or else I don't know who members of the Crisis Staff were, if that's what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's start off with the Crisis Staff president. Did you ever see Blagoje Simic enter the Crisis Staff -- enter the municipal building located next door to the police station during that month that you had to report to the police station? So we're talking about on or about April 21st to May 16th or 17th, during that time, did you ever see Blagoje Simic enter the building, the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me see if this refreshes your recollection. I'm reading from page 4 of your signed, sworn statement, to the Office of the Prosecutor. "It was also known to me that Vaso Antic and Ljubimir Cordasevic who was a journalist at the radio station were attending meetings at the municipal building every morning before the commencement of the radio broadcasts. The other people present at the meetings were the president of the municipality, Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Cedo Simic, the fourth Simic, whose first name I do not know, as well as other members of the Crisis Staff. I used to see them entering the municipal building when I was on my way to report daily to the SUP." Now, you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, sir, in 1998. And you told the truth in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you tried to recall and help as best as you could when you were asked questions.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, however, you asked me specifically about Blagoje Simic, whether I had seen him. I cannot remember sitting here whether I did see him or not and I cannot claim with certainty whether I saw Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, or this fourth Simic. A long time has elapsed for me to be able to remember whether I saw him and where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that this statement, when this statement was taken some five years ago, your memory was fresher because it was closer to the incidents which occurred? It was closer to 1992? And it's now five years later. So wouldn't your memory have been fresher or better back then?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: There are certain details that -- dating from 20 years back that I can remember better than those that transpired two years ago. Well, I don't know. What I do remember at present is what I am actually telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who do you remember walking in to the municipal building? Which members of the civilian authorities that you can recall, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, five years ago, you recalled Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Cedo Simic, and a fourth Simic. Is that Simeon Simic? "And a fourth Simic whose name I don't know and I used to see them entering the municipal building when I was on my way to my daily reporting at the SUP." When you said that back then, you were telling the truth? That was your honest impression at the time, isn't that correct? You weren't lying to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not lying today either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I'm just saying you were telling the truth back then. You weren't being dishonest with them, you weren't trying to fool them when you provided that information. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And concerning the people who were coming and going from the municipal building, your memory apparently was much better five years ago than it is today because you could recall certain details back then that you can't recall anymore?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that there is no reason to doubt your former statement that Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Cedo Simic, and the fourth Simic, were entering and exiting the municipal building and that you saw them do that. There's no reason to doubt your previous statement because you weren't lying to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. When I said, there's no reason to doubt, I asked you a double question. Basically, my question is: When you gave that statement, you were telling the truth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, let's move on. You're familiar with a man by the name of Naser Sejdic [Realtime transcript read in error "Nasa Sedjic"], a policeman?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know Naser from the municipality Bosanski Samac, you know him?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: From the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also know that he had a brother Jusuf who was in the 4th Detachment? He had a brother Jusuf?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sometime after you had been arrested or sometime while you were working at the radio station, you realised that Naser Sejdic was working as a policeman, had returned to work as a policeman in the Bosanski Samac police station under Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you spoke, sir, in Derventa to Zvonko Susic, you indicated that Naser Sejdic mistreated people in Bosanski Samac in his role as a policeman, and I'd like to ask you some questions about that. Do you recall saying that back then?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: In Derventa?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I was never in Derventa with Zvonko. I don't know who Zvonko Susic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do, sir -- do you recall -- let's take a step back. You were aware that Naser Sejdic was arresting people in Samac while he served as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: During the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, during the war.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I didn't see, but I heard from some other prisoners. I didn't personally see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me, just in order not to bring about confusion, here all along the transcript, we talk about Nasa Sedjic. His correct name, if I'm correct, is Naser Sejdic. Not Sedjic and not Nasa. Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm not very good with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're aware or you had heard from fellow prisoners that Naser Sejdic arrested them?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: That he was in the group which detained these people, took them in custody into the police station. Some of my future colleagues who were then detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these people that Naser Sejdic was in the group that arrested were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was also in the group or he himself transported them to the Detention Centre, whether it was the SUP or Zasavica, either he was the driver or he was part of the escort after they were arrested that escorted them to a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You also heard that Naser Sejdic threatened people? You were told by your fellow arrestees, Muslims and Croats, that he had threatened them?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also learned from your fellow colleagues or fellow arrestees that he was mentally harassing them?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I heard that once, he had a bit to drink and went there, but he didn't really beat them up. He was just telling them something. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was harassing them in some manner? Although he didn't physically punch them or beat them, he harassed them verbally?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. The witness just said that he didn't say what he told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: His statement was: "He really didn't beat them up. He was just telling them something."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get some clarification to what was happening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated -- let's take a step back. Where does this incident happen? Did this happen at one of the detention facilities, like the primary school, the high school, the SUP, the TO?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I was at the TO, and this reportedly happened at SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Naser Sejdic had gone there after he had had a few drinks and he made some verbal statements which upset one or more prisoners.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I know you don't know directly, but that's what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, you don't recall. All right, thank you. Now, let's move on a bit. Sometime in mid-May, you're imprisoned at the high school.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at this point, when you get there, there are three to four hundred Croat men being held in addition to you.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew these men, or a number of them, as locals from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And these were civilians from the villages of Gornji Hasici, Donja Hasici, Zasavica? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were there any from any other areas, from Samac or from the town of Samac, or any other locations, Crkvina, or mainly those three that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: There were some from Novo Selo, Tisina, Tursinovac, and Samac, mostly those places where there were Croats. There were also some Croats from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had learned from them that not only had they been locked up in the high school, but their families, meaning their wives and children had been sent to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having worked at the radio station and having heard the daily news, you were aware that these imprisonments occurred after the Serbs or just after the Serbs in Odzak were imprisoned, the imprisonments of the Croats occurred just after the Serbs in Odzak were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, in terms of time period, it's very difficult for me to assess it at present. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it be right about that time? Both things were happening about the same time, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I cannot determine precisely, but maybe approximatively one before the other -- well, no, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, no problem. Now, at the high school, conditions weren't very good. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you agree that there weren't beds and blankets and sheets and towels for all three to four hundred Croat men plus yourself?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me that most of the prisoners were beaten on at least one occasion, whether it was once, some were beaten more than once? But at least most of the prisoners had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, on one occasion, when Lugar and some other paramilitaries visited, most of the prisoners were beaten on that occasion, approximately 250 prisoners were beaten on that occasion. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were also present when Lugar and his fellow paramilitary named Zvezdan appeared and they murdered two civilians from either Donji or Gornji Hasici?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they shot both of them? One was shot either in the head, and the other either in the body or the head?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Since all of us received at least one hit by Lugar, I was able to see myself when he killed one of them, but Zvezdan did not shoot at anyone. And I think it's the same Zvezdan who was arrested now in Belgrade. He didn't shoot at anyone. Now, whether Lugar killed the other one as well or whether it was the other policeman who guarded us, well, this is something I do not know to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that Zvezdan was the one that was arrested recently in Belgrade. Is he alleged to be the assassin of President Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, that question won't be answered by the witness, Mr. Weiner. You're getting outside the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were present, though, when these two people were killed. You didn't see who killed the second one but both were murdered at the high school. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The witness isn't receiving any sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for the end of translation. There wasn't enough time for the interpretation to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Although you didn't see who shot the second man, you were aware that two men were murdered at the high school by Lugar and some -- one of his men or associates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're basically testifying today off your memory. You have no notes or diary or any records of any of the happenings at the high school or the radio station? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that Simo Zaric had never visited the radio station? You testified to that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: His evidence was that he never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That you never saw Simo Zaric at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because it makes a world of a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You never saw Simo Zaric at the radio station. That's what you testified to today. But you're aware, because from counsel -- that in your previous statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998, you indicated that Simo Zaric visited the radio station on page 4, and you initialled that. You initialled the page that Simo Zaric visited the radio station. Could you tell us the reason for the difference, where in 1998 you said Simo Zaric visited the radio station, and today you testify that he didn't, or you never saw him at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember today, I did not see him at the radio station, that I actually saw him there. Whether he was there outside the working hours, well, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you talked about the TV Novi Sad show that you took the audio portion of and made an audiotape?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Novi Sad tape that you took the audio portion off and you made an audiotape so it could be broadcasted on Radio Samac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the information that was contained in that tape? Do you recall what the tape was about? I remember that your father-in-law was actually one of the persons on the tape.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Let me help you a little. I still have this tape at my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're familiar -- you have to be very familiar with the tape. And you recall that Simo Zaric -- first Colonel Nikolic speaks, and then Simo Zaric gives several statements on the tape?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I watched this tape in 1992, and then in -- I don't know, was it 1996 or not? And not after that. But whatever the case, I have it. I have it at home and I can watch it again when I return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you recall a few statements that were made, and we refer to the transcripts of that tape as Exhibit 16A. Do you recall the tape starting off where the journalists talks about an attempted genocide against the Serbs? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 16A ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. For one thing, it is absolutely irrelevant whether the witness remembers or not. We have seen this tape in this Court. We have a transcript of the interview what was on -- everything what was in it. Asking him whether he remembers this portion or that portion, it's irrelevant. It's not in content what was on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the exhibit already before the Trial Chamber, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I want to ask him about some of the statements that were made which are highly inflammatory, statements which incite violence. And I want to ask him about his concerns and if he ever confronted Simo Zaric about Simo Zaric's highly inflammatory and inciteful statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's only fair to put the exhibit before the witness or to show -- I don't know how you're going to do it. But at least put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 16A ter

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Weiner, whether it might be preferable to actually just watch those couple of minutes of the actual video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I thought of that, but they are all in different places. If the Court would like to watch maybe the first five minutes and follow along with the transcript, if you feel that would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean the excerpts you wanted to refer the witness to are in different places?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it may be one here, then one maybe two pages later, then one a page later. So I was just going to refer only to two or three of them

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Right. But you can take the witness through the transcript because you would be able to refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I thought we could do it much quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at the first page where it begins and it talks about, if you look at the opening sentence, it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the text be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Placed on the ELMO because they would also like to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the document in front of you, do you see how it begins, the first page, the opening sentence from the journalist: "A massacre of the population of Serbian nationality and all Muslims who rose to defend the Serbian people"? And then if you look at the third sentence, go to the third sentence done where it begins with "what was the role of the SDA..." "What was the role of the SDA Party of Democratic Action leaders and the Republic of Croatia in the attempted genocide against the Serbs?" Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did I read that correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We are watching something completely different on the screen. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the second page, page 2, Colonel Nikolic talks -- says: "Here in front of me are the photographs of children with helmets, chequered flags, and guns. You can show up a close-up of these pictures later, but I just want to tell you that in Orasje, for example, weapons were distributed even to children who attended a school for the mentally retarded." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page. I just want to refer to a few paragraphs of Simo Zaric's comments. "In the past few days, all information from the field suggested that something very bad was in store for the town and its people." If you go down to the second sentence, the end of the second sentence where it talks about "turning it," meaning Bosanski Samac, "into a war-torn town and the slaughtering of the Serbian and Muslim people who had jointly formed this Territorial Defence." And then the last one, if we can just go to the next page and we're finished, page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The translation that we are receiving is not accurate. If we could have it straight from the ELMO because there are some words that were missed here. It was just that Serbian and Muslim people were supposed to be killed. This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The translation is from the translation department, "slaughtering the Serbian and Muslim people who had jointly formed this Territorial Defence unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is now correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the last one, page 4. Now, this Simo Zaric speaking: "I must say that the special units of the Territorial Defence and the Serbian police did a good job. Time will show that this was good -- this was for the good of the people. They planned sabotage activities throughout the town. You'll be able to see this, too. But they planned assassinations, ambushes, surprise attacks, raids of various" - it can't be read, it's unintelligible - "and other actions against members of the Territorial Defence including the execution of their families and the destruction of the people in charge and their property so as to prevent them from getting in the way of attaining their objectives." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the translation is not a hundred per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which way, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the text back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the translation please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, if we can get the text on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can you put it back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Beginning with the word "Medutim," could the translators please read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Yes, I have to say, however, that the special units of the Territorial Defence and the special units of the Serb police had done this job. The time [Realtime transcript read in error "town"] will show it in favour of these people. Their plan says that they should have resorted to sabotage actions throughout the town. Here you will be able to see it, to organise assassinations, ambushes, attacks, et cetera, against the Territorial Defence, liquidation of the families, destruction of the most responsible people, not people in charge, and the property which would be placed in their way so that they wouldn't persist in pursuing those goals."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's page 63, line 13. Instead of word "the town," the proper word should be "the time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you smirked or kind of laughed when some of these were being read. You were aware that this stuff wasn't true; this was just more propaganda. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Whether it's true or not is up to you to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you knew in April and May of 1992, you knew it was a very tense time in Bosanski Samac, people were being arrested, people were being beaten, people were being murdered. You knew that was a very serious and tense time. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in this tense situation, were you concerned that Simo Zaric's and Colonel Nikolic's statements, where they talk about slaughtering and exterminating families, that that could incite violence or inflame the Serb population against the non-Serbs? Were you concerned about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must object to this question for the simple reason that the question starts with the situation prior to the 17th, and then ends with the situation which is taking place because this interview was on the 29th. So could my learned friend clarify these matters, prior to the conflict when Mr. Zaric and Colonel Nikolic delivered their speeches, and what was in this interview which took place 12 or 13 days after the events in Bosanski Samac. I think that this is simply confounding the witness. The witness is at a loss what period of time he's being asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified that April and May were very tense times in Bosanski Samac, and we talked about murders and arrests and beatings, including yourself. Were you concerned that the broadcasting of those phrases from Simo Zaric and Colonel Nikolic about slaughters, genocide against the Serbian people, extermination of Serbian families, were you concerned that that would incite violence or inflame the Serbs against the non-Serbs or incite violence against the non-Serbs? Were you or your fellow citizens concerned about that?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to be concerned about everything because I was arrested as early as the 18th, so that what I've read, what I've understood, that was 10 or maybe 12 days after my arrest. That is, some people were already arrested and a large number had been arrested by the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But the fact that you were being held, as were others, and people were being beaten while in confinement and being mistreated, and you were severely mistreated in confinement, were you worried that by playing this over and over, it could incite the Serb officers, it could lead to violence against the non-Serb population? Because they're talking about -- or Simo Zaric is talking about threatening a genocide against the Serb population. So did this concern you at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I must just add one thing here, and this is what I -- Mr. Zaric was referring in this portion both to Muslim and Serbian population. And this is here in Document P16. And he was referring to members of the army of Serbian and Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The genocide was mentioned only by the journalist. It can be seen by checking of the transcript of the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, I think it's better to be precise in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you worried in any tape that concerned slaughtering people who were Serbs or Muslims in the 4th Detachment, which is a small portion of Muslims in the municipality of Samac, were you worried that that would have a negative effect or that that could incite violence against the non-Serbs, especially those who were in jail, those who were being held? Weren't you concerned about that, that it could inflame such activity in this tense situation?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Why, of course I was afraid. Who wouldn't be afraid if you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever say to your friend Simo Zaric, "What are you trying to do? These inflammatory statements are going to get us killed?" Did you ever say that to your friend Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. He already said that he didn't see Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the radio station. I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the station. My colleague first should establish whether he saw Simo Zaric after this broadcast, and then he needs to -- this is how he had to find out whether he ever had a possibility to speak to Simo about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He can say that he never saw Simo Zaric, so he never had this discussion. Or maybe he can say he did say it to Simo Zaric. We'll know in just one answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, I couldn't say to Simo anything because I didn't see him because he didn't come to visit me -- I mean, he didn't come to the place where I was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you know that nowhere in that video does it indicate, does it say in that video that Serb authorities are illegally arresting, detaining, and mistreating prisoners. There's no statement like that in the video. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: It is, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is a statement in the video that Serb forces are illegally arresting, detaining, and mistreating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, in the video, Simo Zaric compliments the Serbian police for doing a good job, the same Serbian police who were beating and mistreating prisoners including yourself?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, your time. You've gone beyond 15 minutes actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can I wrap up or is that over now or what would you like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Two minutes. All right. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, just very quickly. Just a few questions. We talked about Naser Sejdic, and you indicated that he was your neighbour. Did he say anything to you -- just checking, did you speak to you prior to your testifying here? Did you have any conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. And you've had no discussion with him by telephone or any other way?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you indicated that you've known Simo Zaric for some 30 years.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, not 30 years, but 15, 16 possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And sir, you indicated you have a business. Are you still doing business in Samac? Does your business sell things or rent things or have sales or business in Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have a shop in Samac. I don't have any businesses in Samac. I'm self-employed in Slovenia, in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you do any sales to garages or gas stations in Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. Not in Samac. Across Bosnia, Croatia, and in Slovenia, what I do is petrol stations, equipment for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you do no business at all in Samac? No business at all in Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He already answer that had question, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the last question, sir, you still have relatives and family that live in Samac?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I thank the Court for giving me the extra minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have a couple of questions related to events mentioned by the Prosecutor in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tihic. My name is Mr. Krgovic, and I am counsel for Miroslav Tadic, and on behalf of Mr. Tadic's defence, I will ask you some questions in relation to some of the answers you gave the Prosecutor. You testified that together with Ibrahim Salkic, you walked in front of a car inviting people to hand over their weapons. Do you remember saying that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, except it wasn't a car, it was a Praga.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Praga. Were you with Salkic all the time, or did you ever separate during that?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: All that time, from the arrest until they put us back in the rooms again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you went with Salkic collecting weapons, did you see Miroslav Tadic on that occasion, that day?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a certain number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tihic, I'm lawyer Pantelic, and I'm counsel for Dr. Blagoje Simic. Very briefly, I have a few topics I wish to cover. Tell me, when you gave your statement to the Prosecution in 1998, the Prosecutor didn't ask you, but I will ask you that now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Sorry, did you say 1998? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Today, the Prosecutor also asked you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, when he asked you allegedly about people who entered the municipal hall and so on and so forth, tell me, did you know then, in 1992, that the seat of the Crisis Staff was in point in fact on the premises of the heating plant, not in the municipal hall? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what the Prosecutor put the pressure on you, whether your memory was better then or now, is it only your assumption that your people were at the meeting or is it a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I didn't put pressure on him, and he's asking about his memory, was it an assumption. He has no memory now, and we read in his prior statement as to his observations. Those aren't assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, Mr. Weiner is right and it's important to be polite to fellow counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do apologise. Maybe it was kind of a language construction which was not proper. I do apologise once again. It was not my intention to be unpolite to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, so in the statement that was quoted to you by the Prosecutor when he said Simic 1, Simic 2, Simic 3, and Simic 4, and so on and so forth, that they attended those meetings which were also attended by Antic and Cordasevic. Is it a fact that you stand by or is it just a guess, a construct, that perhaps people had gone into the municipal hall on some other business? Will you explain it to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As I went to work, Mr. Antic and Mr. Cordasevic during a formal conversation said they had been to the Crisis Staff in the municipal hall, and then as they talked between them, I learned more or less who had been there. So that was that. So to this day, I don't know who was the member of the Crisis Staff, that is, who were other members and who was what. All I know is that the president was -- I mean, during the conversation, that the president -- I learned that the president was Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I see. Your Honour, I believe it's time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, the last question related to this subject before we went off the break, you and Cordasevic, et cetera, do you remember that subject? So as we read this statement of yours, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber now, did you see Antic and Cordasevic entering the municipality building when you were going to the police station? Is that the essence of your answer?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Counsel is now confusing two different pieces of testimony. The first thing -- and this is an improper area of cross-examination. Number one, I asked this witness who he recalled entering the building. All he recalled were two people, the two people he worked with. With regard to civilian authorities, he had no memory or recollection. I then attempted to refresh his recollection with his statements. He still had no memory of who entered. The third thing I tried to do is I asked him if his statements that he made were true. He didn't recall what statements he had made. He said he told the truth to the Office of the Prosecutor, but he had no memory of even the statements he made here. Now, counsel is trying to cross-examine. Did you mean this in relation to the statements that you don't even recall? Do you mean that in relation to the statements that you do not recall? He can't do that. He has no memory. He has testified to that. The most he can say is: Did you tell the truth? Did you have a better memory back then? Did you know more details back then? Were you truthful? That's all we were able to get out of him. But to question him as to the details of something he doesn't remember is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, the -- to some extent, part of this statement is confusing. It's double-barrelled, it is something which is not clear, so that's why I want to clarify. I agree with my learned friend absolutely with the position of the witness. We all heard what he said. But in this particular statement, it is not clear whether this witness saw Antic and Cordasevic entering a building or Simic 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. That's the basis I would like to clarify because it was raised through the questions of my learned friend, simply as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You can't clarify what you don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This is what Mr. Weiner said. That's precisely -- he now cannot recall that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will go to the other topic, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, let us cover another subject now. When the Prosecutor asked you about the secondary school where you were detained and whether there were any locals from the surrounding villages, you mentioned Gornji Hasici, et cetera, and some other villages where the detainees came from. Tell me now, when talking to those people then or perhaps from contacts that you had with the guards, do you have any knowledge and if so, please tell the Trial Chamber, whether anybody mentioned the attack against Serb soldiers in those villages at that time, that they had sustained some casualties in May 1992, that they had been wounded or killed or something like that? Do you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next, when you went to the exchange, did you say to this investigator in Derventa that as you were travelling for the exchange, I assume to Dragalic, that you saw a large number of Croat civilians in the villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The villages were read out too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Object. That's outside the scope of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, nothing was raise about the witness going to the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but this official note when this witness gave his statement, so that was the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It wasn't raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, Mr. Tihic, tell me, you are a media person from the radio, you have experience in this area, the Prosecutor asked you about certain expressions used during the war, derogatory terms, Ustasha, Chetnik, et cetera. Please tell the Trial Chamber, what is your personal knowledge in that period while you were able to follow these programmes? Did all three sides use these, how should I put this, heavy words in respect of the others?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I worked only on one side, so I could hear only one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since this is a neighbouring -- this is a border area, could other radio stations be heard in Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly, but I did not have the opportunity of hearing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your personal knowledge regarding this particular subject just before the conflict broke out and in that period, did all three parties in a way put down the other sides? I mean, I'm interested in the vocabulary used in the media, on television, et cetera. Can you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: A year and a half before the conflict broke out, I went from the radio station to the power company. Ever since -- rather, until the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords, I never turned on my radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we've received sufficient evidence on the rising tensions among the ethnic groups. So we don't need to ask this witness any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I believe it's a not disputed fact that all three parties during the war are -- make some references with regard to the inflammatory speeches or words. I believe that it's not in dispute in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you made your statement to the Prosecutor in 1998, you used the expression "Chetniks" in reference to the Serb side a few times, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, on page 4 of your statement, you say: "While I was at the radio station, Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric, and the other Chetniks would visit and order me to play Chetnik music." So you also used these expressions that are a bit harsh?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So these are not your words?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I mean, I said Chetniks because they themselves proclaimed themselves as such because I was taping some songs recording them for them, for some of these people who came up there, I mean. Those are the kinds of songs that I recorded and rerecorded for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The last question related to the subject that was raised by the Prosecutor. These are the so-called propaganda lies, false news, and things like that. You already referred to this, but do you remember what were the news related to the number of Serb casualties, because there was a war in Samac at the time? Do you remember the figures? What did the news say? How many Serbs got killed?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: A smaller number. A smaller number got killed. And that the enemy had sustained more casualties. That's the way it was roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, these details don't help us at all in the case as to how many Serbs, how many Muslims were killed, how many. There was an armed conflict; that is agreed by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, Your Honour, because I almost finished. My question was related to the theory, Prosecution theory, that there was some kind of propaganda, war propaganda, and false news on the radio station of Samac, including a number of killed or wounded Serbian soldiers, et cetera, et cetera. So I just want to clarify that, whether it was false propaganda or it was a fact. Simply as that because my understanding is that was the Prosecution theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to him asking about propaganda, but it's not the Prosecution theory. It's his testimony. It's the evidence that's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just last question, and I'm finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just clarify this one thing: The news said that less Serbs were killed than in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that more enemy soldiers were killed than in real life?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an example. If five Serbs would get killed, then they would say it was less, and then if 20 enemy soldiers would get killed, then they would again change the figure to show that it was even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, we need to clarify a few things, and I hope that we will finish soon. You said here to the Prosecutor that you've known Mr. Simo Zaric for some 15 or 16 years. Were you and Mr. Zaric members of the hunting organisation called Fazan, pheasant, and did you hunt together one group?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of your hunting group?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In that group, was there a larger number of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Vlado Sisic was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean Vlado Sisic and Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Pisarevic please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, in that hunting group of yours, there were two Serbs, one was Simo Zaric and the other one was Vlado Sisic?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you know that the 4th Detachment existed.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about Mr. Zaric before the conflict calling upon members of all ethnic groups to respond to mobilisation of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Whether he called upon people to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any obstacles in your path if you wished to join the 4th Detachment as a member of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity of hearing Simo Zaric over the media or at gatherings of citizens or at peace rallies or things like that? I'm talking about before the war.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the war. I think that once there was this one gathering over there near the committee, and that I was there once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Where this was talked about, that there should be reconciliation, things like that, along those lines. I mean I can't really remember now because it was such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You remember that as far as this reconciliation is concerned and the easing of tensions, easing of interethnic tensions, that Mr. Zaric spoke about these things. Right?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you were arrested on the 18th, can you remember since you mentioned here that Stevan Todorovic handed you and Ibela Salkic over to the 4th Detachment? Do you remember who the persons were that you were handed over to at the police station? Was it perhaps Cviko Tesic, nicknamed Cvikan?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: He was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't hand us over directly to anyone. He was there, among other people, Cvikan, and he said that we should go there as it was put --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: From the police station to the building of the local community where the flag of the Red Cross was, did you cover that part of the road on foot or by car?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And then, you went with the members of the 4th Detachment to collect weapons. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, I'm going to repeat this. This person I mentioned is Cviko Tesic nicknamed Cvikan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one matter, this vehicle that went behind you, it was not a tank. Right?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had it been a tank, you would have certainly known it was a tank?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, at least I know that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, now, while you were collecting these weapons, did you or any one of the members of the 4th Detachment enter anybody's apartment or search anybody's apartment or house?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No. Whoever had weapons handed them over, and those who didn't, didn't. So in fact, we only collected weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you pick out houses selectively in terms of this is a Muslim, a Croat, a Serb house, this one we will take, this one we won't, or did you actually systematically go from each house to another house or from a flat to a flat?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Since we knew who -- the houses and who they belonged to in Samac, we just went to -- on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You went to all of them?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was any coercion applied in respect of the citizens in Samac? Did anyone threaten anybody, any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in a position to, nor did they threaten. It was simply -- I don't know if it was out of fear, but whoever had any weapons handed them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While collecting these weapons, did you see Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You were explaining the encounter with Mr. Simo Zaric at the police station. Could you describe this in more detail, how did this encounter take place and how did Mr. Zaric treat you, in a friendly, unfriendly way, or in a patronising way, as if meeting a subordinate? How did this encounter take place? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: When we were going out of the office of Stevan Todorovic, I saw him come out of the room on the left-hand side, and he took me to the -- this room on the left-hand side, and he told me: "Come, you should come and see some of the documents and what they were doing." I asked what was it all about. And then he showed me the documents allegedly found in the desk of Naser Sejdic [as interpreted] and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just let me ask you, were you afraid of seeing Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. I was happy to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that Namik Suljic left Samac, and that he left his wife and children there?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I was cautioned here about a mistake in the name. The Naser Sejdic's name is reflected here but we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, Namik Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Simo Zaric was angry in a way of Namik for having left his children and wife because he was -- he had to take care of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. I object, number one, it's leading. Number two, whether or not he's angry, how is that relevant to the issues and I never got into any of Namik Suljic's personal situation, only as to the threats that Simo Zaric made against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw this question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you were not afraid of Simo Zaric when he took you to see these lists and when he told you all about it?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He already answered that question, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the detained persons that you had contacts with and so on express any complaint concerning the treatment by Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. No one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if someone said that the detention of people was carried out by the military or the police or by those in the camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: The police and those in the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You and the other people who were detained, were you afraid of Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: I said this already once. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you talked about yourself. I'm asking about the others.

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: No, no, they weren't. I know with reliability that they weren't afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought you were finished. That's why you kept on repeating the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I just have two small questions. You mentioned that you were ordered by Stevan Todorovic to go with members of the 4th Detachment and remove the Red Cross flag from the Red Cross offices. I'm just wondering, have you any idea, do you know, in other words, why you were ordered to remove the Red Cross flag; and once you were done so, what did you and Mr. Salkic do with it?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: From the very start, there must have been a mistake. We were not ordered to take down the Red Cross flag because it seemed to bother someone, but because we were supposed to take this Red Cross flag and hold it and carry it front of the Praga as some sort of a mark or identification and go on collecting weapons this way. So apart from having those patches, that is armbands, we carried the Red Cross flag as some sort of a recognition sign -- I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay, that makes a little bit more sense now. And the second question actually concerns this Praga vehicle. Do you remember whether this Praga had what are called caterpillars, like a tank, or whether it simply had ordinary tyres like you would find on a truck or a car?

utterances.speaker: PASAGA TIHIC
utterances.text: It seems to me, as far as I can remember, that it had large tyres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic, for giving evidence. You are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you allow me just two very brief issues I would like to address the Chamber. On Friday, last Friday, the Trial Chamber made its ruling with regard to the testimony of Mr. Cedomir Simic. After the withdrawal on the part of the Defence and consent of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber ruled that he should come here and give his viva voce testimony, actually only cross-examination limited to one hour. Initially, when the Defence proposed to withdraw -- to withdraw the witness, Mr. Simic, Cedomir Simic, our understanding was that in case that the ruling of Trial Chamber would be opposite or other than the proposal of the Defence, I believe that we should have a possibility to have him in chief for a certain number of -- for an hour, maybe half an hour or hour. So it was quite limited. My understanding was when we were of the opinion to withdraw him, then that's conditionally if he will come, then the previous ruling of the Trial Chamber will be in force, which means that the Defence will have time to question him, and also Prosecution for the cross-examination. I just want to clarify that with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. When you withdrew him, you withdrew him in total. It would have meant even the Rule 92 bis statement being withdrawn. The Trial Chamber decided that his evidence was essential, and decided that it should remain, his evidence should remain on record, and then he can come for cross-examination only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay, Your Honour. I understand that. But initially your ruling was that also Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- is entitled to have him for a certain number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, initially, yes, he was supposed to give viva voce evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the interests of justice, maybe it would be proper now to have -- because now we are at the beginning of the case I would say in this particular issue I'm speaking, that the Defence would be entitled in the interests of justice to have him here for examination-in-chief, and then Prosecution will proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you want is to reinstate the previous order?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That's correct. Because otherwise, we'll be -- it will not be fair to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection if counsel wants to question their own witness, however the Court wants to do it, we have no objection if counsel wants to do an examination-in-chief or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber will give its ruling in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And another matter I would like to bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber, the fact with regard to the travel arrangements for our demographic experts and two associates of her. I do believe -- I mean, just to keep you informed because maybe we should be in problem with a certain schedule problems, we shall know that during this afternoon, that I believe that the registry will take all necessary measures to obtain a visa for these three members of the team, expert team to come here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought that those matters normally are taken care of by the registry. We don't need to discuss them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The other thing the Trial Chamber wanted to ask you, you presented the last batch of the 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are no longer calling Drago Sego; Momir Talic, for instance, you are supposed to take a statement; and Mr. Krajisnik. So you've decided to withdraw these?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you mention Mr. Krajisnik, General Talic, and I didn't catch the first one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Drago Sego.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Sego.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to check that. It's not seems that it was my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the last statements that the Trial Chamber did order that they be recorded during the week beginning 17th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the top of my head, I cannot recollect that Drago Sego was my client. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you look into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will check that and I will inform tomorrow accordingly the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For Simo Zaric, there is supposed to be Witness X and Witness Y and Ecimovic. Are these now dropped off the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We shall not be calling those witnesses, and I can explain why we will not call them. Witness X, we're not going to call that witness because after interviewing him -- during our interviews with him, he requested that he be remunerated for lost profits, and we could not discuss that so that we have given up on him. Mr. Ecimovic, likewise. He does not seem to be willing to come to The Hague for reasons of his own. And Witness Amir Dervic will not be called either to testify before this Honourable Court. So that we have the witnesses under Rule 92. It is five witnesses altogether, and they should testify this week, that is, they should testify before this Honourable Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next witness. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the redacted version of Witness 92 statement has just been provided for the Trial Chamber and for our colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's important for us to use the correct terms, that the statement now without the paragraphs that were struck out. Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOPOLOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOPOLOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you just please come -- bring your chair closer to the microphone so that we could hear you also. Thank you very much. Sir, during your proofing, I already warned you that you should wait with your answers, that is, to wait for me to finish the question, then wait a couple of seconds before you start answering so as to avoid speaking over one another and so that the interpreters could do their job properly and so that everything that you say is recorded. So have you understood me? Wait for me to finish the question, count one or two seconds, and then start answering.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOPOLOVAC
utterances.text: Very well, yes. I've understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, will you say for the transcript your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOPOLOVAC
utterances.text: My name is Mihajlo Topolovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in December 2002, you made a written statement and signed it in front of the representatives of the registry of this Tribunal in Bosanski Samac. Your statement has been tendered into evidence, and the Trial Chamber has decided to hear you viva voce with regard to information to some parts of your statement so that my questions will bear only on what has been struck out from your statement, that is, deleted, and you are to testify about that today. The last thing you spoke about in your statement before the part that was struck out was paragraph 24 of your statement. In that paragraph, you speak about the situation -- about the state of affairs in the police station, how the members of special units seized valuables from the detainees, took them to houses and looted. Have you heard about the beating of prisoners and that Stevan Todorovic hinted that you and others should do things like that, but that you had refused? So we are in the police station. The Trial Chamber already knows how you got there and what you did there. Now, I'd like to ask you something in relation to Mr. Zaric.
